definition: The part of the upper atmosphere, from about 60 to 400 km up, where sunlight frees electrons from the air. It can bend HF radio waves back down to Earth.
A radio wave that goes up, is bent back down by the ionosphere and reaches the ground far away, sometimes after several bounces.
A radio wave that follows the curve of the Earth's surface. At HF it only reaches a few tens to a few hundred kilometres.
The ring around an HF transmitter where nothing is heard: too far for the ground wave, too close for the first sky wave to come back down.
The highest frequency an ionospheric layer sends back when you transmit straight up. Slanting waves are returned at higher frequencies.
The highest frequency the ionosphere will bend back to reach a particular place at a particular time. Above it, the waves escape into space.
A frequency a little below the MUF (about 85 % of it) that gives a strong, reliable HF path with a safety margin.
The lowest part of the ionosphere, about 60 to 90 km up. It exists only in daylight and absorbs HF waves, the lower frequencies most.
The highest ionospheric layer, about 250 to 400 km up (F1 and F2 by day, one merged F layer at night). It is the main mirror for long-distance HF.
Selective calling: the ground station sends a four-letter code as two pairs of tones, and only the aircraft with that code rings a chime, so pilots do not have to listen to HF noise all the time.
A kind of AM that sends only one half of the voice signal and leaves out the carrier, so all the power goes into a narrow channel. HF aviation voice uses the upper sideband.
A sudden burst of energy from the Sun. Its X-rays make the D layer absorb strongly on the sunlit side of the Earth, blacking out HF for minutes to hours.
Crackles and crashes in a radio caused mainly by lightning, which can be heard thousands of kilometres away on HF. It is worst at low frequencies.
One trip of an HF wave up to the ionosphere and back down to the Earth. Long paths use several hops, bouncing off the sea in between.
Sending short data messages, such as position reports and text messages, over HF radio instead of voice. Used where satellites are not available.
